# The packages that hold the project to its claims

<!-- Generated by tools/handbook. Edit the code, not this file. -->

<!-- kind: reference -->

These packages contain tests and almost no product code. Each reads the
repository (the specification, the ledger, the documentation, the build policy,
the module registry) and fails when two things that must agree do not. They are
the reason a claim in this handbook is a checked claim.

Each entry below is the package's own documentation comment, unedited, followed by
the files it is made of and what it exports. The comments in this codebase are long on
purpose: they say why, and why the obvious alternative is wrong.

## `internal/buildpolicy`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/buildpolicy`.

Package buildpolicy enforces the parts of the specification that are about the source tree rather than about behaviour: the lexicon policy of SPEC section 2.3 and the dependency allowlist of section 4.2.

These are tests rather than a separate linter so that \`go test ./...\` fails on a violation, which is what "CI fails the build on a match" means in practice.

**Files:** `lexicon.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Finding` (type): Finding is one prohibited term in one place.
- `IsExempt` (func): IsExempt reports whether a repository-relative path is outside the policy.
- `Scan` (func): Scan walks a tree and reports every prohibited term outside the exemptions.
- `Term` (type): Term is a prohibited word and what to use instead.

## `internal/specaudit`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/specaudit`.

Package specaudit holds SPEC.md and docs/DIVERGENCE.md to each other and to what a build actually ships.

A gap that is not written down is a gap that gets rediscovered, and a gap that is written down and then quietly filled leaves a document that lies. Both are test failures here rather than documentation problems.

**Files:** ; with tests.

## `internal/docsaudit`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/docsaudit`.

Package docsaudit holds the generated reference documentation to the code it was generated from.

docs/configuration.md and docs/modules.md are written by tools/gendocs. Generated documentation that is committed and then not checked is worse than none: it is trusted, and it goes stale the first time someone adds a module and forgets. This fails when a generated file and the code disagree, and the fix is to run the generator.

**Files:** ; with tests.

## `internal/handbook`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/handbook`.

Package handbook turns the Markdown under docs/ into the handbook that ships in every release, and holds that Markdown to the checks that make "always up to date" a property of the build rather than an intention.

### Why there is a Markdown converter in a project with no dependencies

SPEC 4.2 closes the dependency list, and Markdown is not in the Go standard library. The handbook has to be readable in two places that never meet: on GitHub, where it is Markdown, and inside a release archive on a machine with no network, where it has to be something a browser opens. Writing the converter here, for the dialect the documentation actually uses, is a few hundred lines; admitting a library to render prose would be a SPEC change for a tool that ships in no binary.

It is deliberately not CommonMark. It converts the subset the handbook is written in -- ATX headings, paragraphs, fenced code, nested lists, GFM tables, block quotes, inline code, emphasis, links -- and it REFUSES the constructs it does not understand rather than guessing: a line of raw HTML, for instance, is an error naming the line. A renderer that quietly mangles a page it does not understand is the documentation equivalent of a state module that reports success without changing anything.

**Files:** `book.go`, `check.go`, `gen.go`, `index.go`, `known.go`, `markdown.go`, `site.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Book` (type): Book is the parsed manifest and everything rendered from it.
- `Build` (func): Build writes the handbook as HTML: a page per chapter, the contents, the index, and the whole book on one page for searching and printing.
- `BuildIndex` (func): BuildIndex collects the index of a loaded book.
- `CLIChapter` (func): CLIChapter renders the command-line reference from the binaries' own help.
- `Chapter` (type): Chapter is one entry of the book.
- `Check` (func): Check loads the whole book and returns every problem found.
- `CheckGroups` (func): CheckGroups returns what is wrong with the assignment of packages to chapters: a package no chapter describes, one described twice, and one that is named and does not exist.
- `CodeSpan` (type): CodeSpan is one inline `code span`, with the section it appeared in, which is what the automatic index is made of.
- `Contents` (func): Contents renders docs/handbook/README.md: the table of contents, for someone reading on GitHub rather than in the HTML edition.
- `Directive` (type): Directive is an instruction to the build written as an HTML comment, invisible on GitHub: `<!-- index: term; other term -->`.
- `Doc` (type): Doc is a rendered document and what was learned about it on the way.
- `Entry` (type): Entry is one term of the index and everywhere it appears.
- `EventTags` (func): EventTags runs `halite-hub event tags` and returns the tag patterns it prints, the namespace this build fires.
- `EveryPackage` (func): EveryPackage lists the Go packages of the repository that are documented: the directories under cmd, ext, internal and tools that hold Go source.
- `Fence` (type): Fence is one fenced code block.
- `Generate` (func): Generate returns every generated file, keyed by repository-relative path.
- `Group` (type): Group is a run of packages that one generated chapter covers.
- `Heading` (type): Heading is one heading of a document, with the anchor GitHub would give it, so that a link written for one renderer lands in the other.
- `Known` (type): Known is a set of identifiers of one kind that the index recognises when it sees one in a code span: every command, every setting, every module function, every event tag.
- `KnownIdentifiers` (func): KnownIdentifiers collects, from the build itself, the identifiers the index recognises when a chapter puts one in a code span.
- `Link` (type): Link is one link target, as written.
- `Options` (type): Options controls rendering.
- `PackageChapter` (func): PackageChapter renders one group.
- `Part` (type): Part is a run of chapters under one title.
- `Problem` (type): Problem is one thing wrong with the handbook, worded so that the person reading a failed test knows which file to open.
- `ReadContents` (func): ReadContents parses the manifest.
- `Ref` (type): Ref is one place a term is found.
- `Render` (func): Render converts one document.
- `SiteOptions` (type): SiteOptions describes one build of the handbook.
- `Slug` (func): Slug exposes the anchor rule to the checks that resolve links.

## `internal/chaos`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/chaos`.

Package chaos is SPEC 31's chaos layer: the registry of the scenarios the specification names, what each is defined to do, and the guard that holds the two to each other.

The layer was entirely absent until 2026-09-06 — \`grep -i chaos\` over the tree returned nothing — and the argument for building it is not that SPEC asks for it. It is that three defects of one shape were found in a fortnight, all three by accident:

  - the webhook returner's spool named files by a timestamp that is not unique, so a backlog went upstream out of order (4.9);
  - the relay spool did the same and silently overwrote, losing a return in the mechanism whose whole purpose is not to (4.9);
  - the hub's job record was read, changed and written back by two goroutines, so a queued job could be delivered to a node twice (4.11).

Each is correct read one operation at a time and wrong when two arrive together. None of them had a test with two of anything in it. The first two were found by inspection while looking at something else; the third was an intermittent CI failure written off as a flake for a week. That is not a run of bad luck, it is the absence of this layer, and the fourth defect of the shape is presumably in the tree now.

### What a scenario is

SPEC 31's Chaos row names eight and says each must have "a defined, tested, documented behaviour". Three words, and the order matters: the behaviour is decided first and written down here, then a test holds the build to it. A scenario whose Behaviour reads "it depends" has not been through the first step.

Registering one here does not make it true. \`chaos\_test.go\` checks that every scenario SPEC names is registered, that nothing is registered that SPEC does not name, and that each has a test that says it exercises it. What none of that checks is whether the behaviour written down is the behaviour anybody wants.

**Files:** `chaos.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Exercises` (func): Exercises names the scenario a test covers, and is how a test is tied to a row of this registry.
- `Keys` (func): Keys returns every registered key, in registry order.
- `Lookup` (func): Lookup returns a scenario by key.
- `Scenario` (type): A Scenario is one row of SPEC 31's chaos layer.

## `internal/perf`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/perf`.

Package perf is SPEC section 30: the performance targets, what measures each one, and the two that can be measured with a benchmark alone.

SPEC 30 opens by saying the targets are given "with the measurement method, so they can be tested rather than asserted". Until this package existed, \`grep "func Benchmark"\` over the tree returned nothing, so all thirteen rows were asserted and none was tested.

Two of the thirteen name a benchmark as their own method: the highstate compile and the pillar compile. Those two need no simulated fleet, no second machine and no clock discipline beyond \`go test -bench\`, so they are built here. The other eleven need the scale harness, a soak, or an integration matrix, and the table below carries each one with what it waits on, held to SPEC's own table by a guard so that a row cannot be forgotten or quietly reworded.

### What a number from here means

It means one machine compiled one generated tree. It is not a claim about a fleet, and the compile is not the whole of \`state.apply\` -- it is the parse, the render, the requisite resolution and the ordering, which is what SPEC's row names and what a node does before it touches anything.

	make perf

runs the benchmarks and checks the two measured rows against their targets. It is deliberately not part of \`make check\`: a wall clock on a shared CI runner measures the runner, and a gate that fails for that reason gets ignored, which is worse than not having it.

**Files:** ; with tests.

## `internal/saltdiff`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/saltdiff`.

Package saltdiff holds SPEC section 31's differential gate: the same state tree compiled by halite and by Salt, compared.

SPEC 31 names this the primary correctness gate, on the reasoning that no amount of unit testing establishes that an existing tree means the same thing under a reimplementation. Only the reference implementation can say that.

The gate skips, loudly, where Salt is not installed. It must never pass quietly for that reason:

	python3 -m venv /tmp/salt && /tmp/salt/bin/pip install salt
	HALITE_SALT_CALL=/tmp/salt/bin/salt-call go test ./internal/saltdiff/

Set HALITE\_SALTDIFF\_REGEN=1 to print the deviation table.

**Files:** ; with tests.
